questions.stem: Which of the following defines Electronic Protection (EP) as quoted from PAM 3-0702-01?
questions.key: It safeguards personnel, facilities and equipment from the effects of spectrum emissions, whether friendly, adversary or natural
distractors: It attacks the enemy's use of the electromagnetic spectrum
It searches for, intercepts and locates enemy emitters for the commander
It safeguards equipment only from adversary jamming
questions.explanation: EP safeguards personnel, facilities and equipment from the effects of emissions in the spectrum, including friendly, adversary or natural interference.
why: That is Electronic Attack, the new name for ECM.
That is the ES role, not EP.
EP covers friendly and natural interference too, not only adversary jamming.

questions.stem: Which statement matches ECM and ECCM in the terminology used in the deck?
questions.key: ECM is now called Electronic Attack, and ECCM is now called Electronic Protection
distractors: ECM is now called Electronic Protection, and ECCM is now called Electronic Attack
ECM is now called Electronic Support, and ECCM is now called Electronic Protection
ECM is now called Electronic Attack, and ECCM is now called Electronic Support
questions.explanation: Slide 6 states that ECM is now Electronic Attack and ECCM is now Electronic Protection.
why: That swaps the two terms.
ECM is Electronic Attack, not Electronic Support.
ECCM is Electronic Protection, not Electronic Support.

questions.stem: Which of the following describes frequency hopping?
questions.key: The radio jumps channels many times per second in a pattern only friendly radios know
distractors: The signal is spread so that it is harder to detect and jam
A long, coded pulse is squeezed on receive for range detail and anti-jam margin
A second antenna spots jamming arriving from the side so the radar ignores it
questions.explanation: A hopping radio jumps channels many times per second in a pattern only friendly radios know, so a spot jammer hits only a few hops and error correction recovers the rest.
why: That is spread spectrum.
That is pulse compression, a radar technique.
That is sidelobe blanking, a radar technique.

questions.stem: Which of the following describes what encryption protects?
questions.key: WHAT you say, so the enemy hears gibberish
distractors: WHETHER your message gets through despite jamming
WHERE your transmitter is, so direction finding cannot locate it
WHEN your station transmits, so that no pattern forms
questions.explanation: Encryption protects what you say; anti-jam measures protect whether it gets through, and encryption does not hide location.
why: That is the job of anti-jam measures.
The deck states that encryption does not hide location.
Varying the routine, not encryption, breaks up patterns.

questions.stem: It is the EP measure that protects equipment from damaging energy and jamming through shielding, filtering and grounding.
questions.explanation: Hardening protects equipment through shielding, filtering and grounding, checked on every setup through cable shielding, connectors and grounding.
why: Spectrum management keeps our own emitters from jamming each other through assigned frequencies.
Emission control governs what may transmit under given conditions.
Frequency hopping jumps channels in a pattern only friendly radios know.

questions.stem: It is the effect in which a weapon switches to guide on a jamming source, so the jammer becomes a target.
questions.explanation: Some weapons can switch to guiding on a jamming source, which is why a strong emitter, jammer or radio can be located and struck.
why: Sidelobe blanking is a radar technique that ignores jamming arriving from the side.
Frequency agility is a radar technique that changes frequency pulse to pulse.
Spoofing feeds a receiver a wrong position or time.

questions.stem: It is the radar technique in which a second antenna spots jamming arriving from the side, so the radar ignores it.
questions.explanation: Sidelobe blanking uses a second antenna to spot jamming that arrives from the side.
why: Frequency agility changes frequency from pulse to pulse.
Pulse compression squeezes a long, coded pulse on receive.
Low-probability-of-intercept uses low-power, wideband waveforms that are hard for ES to detect.

questions.stem: A battalion is at risk of attack, so it limits transmissions and watches power levels. Which EMCON level is this?
questions.explanation: EMCON 2 YELLOW applies when there is a risk of attack, with limited transmissions and watched power levels.
why: EMCON 1 GREEN is normal operation with no hostile activity.
EMCON 3 AMBER is the field baseline, with encryption, hopping and directional antennas and unencrypted systems off.
EMCON 4 RED applies once an attack has occurred.

questions.stem: Attacks are under way, and the commander orders the most restrictive level, isolating compromised systems. Which EMCON level is this?
questions.explanation: EMCON 5 BLACK is for attacks under way and isolates compromised systems.
why: EMCON 4 RED applies after an attack has occurred, with non-essential emitters off and alternates used.
EMCON 3 AMBER is the field baseline, not the most restrictive level.
EMCON 2 YELLOW only limits transmissions when there is a risk of attack.

questions.stem: A platoon's net fills with static. The signaller disconnects the antenna and the noise drops. What does the lesson say this suggests?
questions.key: The source is outside the radio
distractors: The radio, its cables or its power should be suspected
questions.explanation: If the noise drops when the antenna is disconnected, the source is outside the radio; the cause still has to be worked out among jamming, interference and terrain.
why: That is the conclusion when the noise stays with the antenna disconnected.
That conclusion comes from the move-or-turn check, not the antenna test.
An outside source could still be friendly interference, so jamming is not confirmed.

questions.stem: A convoy's GPS shows a wrong time and a speed reading while the vehicles are halted. Which GPS threat does this suggest?
distractors: A compatibility failure among own emitters
questions.explanation: Wrong time and speed while stationary are spoofing red flags; spoofing gives a wrong fix that looks right.
why: Jamming gives no fix at all rather than a wrong one.
Home-on-jam is a weapon guiding on a jamming source.
A compatibility failure concerns friendly emitters interfering with each other.

questions.stem: A signaller keeps sending radio checks just for comfort when nothing needs reporting. Which radio-discipline rule is being broken?
distractors: Use the lowest power that works
questions.explanation: The deck's rule to transmit only when needed rules out chatter and radio checks for comfort.
why: Lowest power concerns the range of enemy DF.
Short transmissions concern message length, not whether to transmit.
Varying the routine concerns fixed report times and patterns.

questions.stem: Which list contains the five EP measures?
questions.key: Hardening, encryption, frequency hopping, emission control, spectrum management
distractors: Hardening, encryption, frequency hopping, terrain masking, spectrum management
Hardening, encryption, radio discipline, emission control, spectrum management
Shielding, encryption, frequency hopping, emission control, PACE
questions.explanation: The five EP measures are hardening, encryption, frequency hopping, emission control and spectrum management.
why: Terrain masking is a field practice, not one of the five measures.
Radio discipline is a field practice, not one of the five measures.
Shielding is part of hardening and PACE is a continuity plan; neither is a named measure.

questions.stem: Which list gives the seven lines of the generic interference report?
questions.key: WHO, WHEN, WHERE, FREQUENCY / NET, WHAT, EFFECT, ACTIONS
distractors: WHO, WHEN, WHERE, FREQUENCY / NET, WHY, EFFECT, ACTIONS
WHO, WHEN, WHERE, POWER, WHAT, EFFECT, ACTIONS
WHO, WHAT, WHERE, FREQUENCY / NET, CAUSE, EFFECT, ACTIONS
questions.explanation: The deck's generic training report has seven lines: WHO, WHEN, WHERE, FREQUENCY / NET, WHAT, EFFECT and ACTIONS.
why: WHY is not a line; the cause is left unresolved in the report.
POWER is not a line; FREQUENCY / NET is.
CAUSE is not a line, and WHEN is missing.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT one of the four possible causes of sudden static in the ice breaker?
questions.explanation: The four possible causes are enemy jamming, friendly interference, equipment fault, and terrain and distance. Hardening is an EP measure, not a cause.
why: Enemy jamming is one of the four causes.
Equipment fault is one of the four causes.
Terrain and distance is one of the four causes.
